tariffs_and_supply.hts_classification: Electric motorcycles/mopeds: HTSUS 8711.60.00 (8711.60.0050 e-bikes <= 750 W-ish / 8711.60.0090 other). General (MFN) duty: Free. Source: CBP ruling NY N344662 (2024-12-20).
tariffs_and_supply.section_301_base: China-origin 8711.60.0090 carries the Section 301 List 2 additional duty of 25% (Chapter 99 9903.88.02) per NY N344662. FACT.
tariffs_and_supply.section_301_ev_100_percent: The Sept 2024 four-year-review increase to 100% applied to 'electric vehicles' under heading 8703 (passenger cars); our reading is that 8711.60 electric motorcycles were NOT moved to 100% and remain at 25%. UNCERTAIN - we could not open the Federal Register annex; confirm the exact Chapter 99 line with a licensed customs broker before pricing.
tariffs_and_supply.ieepa_tariffs: The 20% 'fentanyl' IEEPA tariff (Mar 2025, later cut to 10% after the Nov 1, 2025 Trump-Xi deal) and the IEEPA 'reciprocal' tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court on 2026-02-20 (6-3) and terminated; refund mechanics are still being worked out (Penn Wharton, White & Case). FACT.
tariffs_and_supply.section_122_and_replacement: A 10% Section 122 balance-of-payments surcharge ran from Feb 2026 and expired 2026-07-24. It was replaced the same minute by new Section 301 'forced-labor' tariffs of 10-12.5% on 60 economies; China is in the 12.5% tier, stacking on top of existing 301 duties (Holland & Knight, Wiley, Akerman, July 2026). FACT.
tariffs_and_supply.section_232_steel_aluminum_derivatives: 8711.60 was added to the steel/aluminum derivative list effective 2025-08-19 (50% on the steel/aluminum content value, not the whole bike). A revised proclamation effective 2026-04-06 removed 'certain finished motorcycles' from the derivative list (Powersports Business 2026-04-09) but did not publish which lines; aftermarket parts still captured at 25%. UNCERTAIN whether 8711.60 finished e-motos are now out.
tariffs_and_supply.batteries_shipped_separately: Section 301 on China-origin non-EV lithium-ion batteries (8507.60) rose from 7.5% to 25% on 2026-01-01 (plus 3.4% MFN). Spare/replacement 74V packs imported separately face ~28% + 12.5% forced-labor. FACT.
tariffs_and_supply.estimated_current_stack_china_built_emot: ESTIMATE (Sep 2026): 0% MFN + 25% (301 List 2) + 12.5% (301 forced-labor) = ~37.5% of customs value, plus any residual 232 content duty; this matches the ~37.5% 'effective China rate' quoted by trade-tool sites for most machinery. Down from ~55-57.5% in mid-2025 (when 20% IEEPA + 10% reciprocal applied) but still ~3x the 2024 level. Exclusions extended to 2026-11-10 under the Nov 2025 US-China deal do not cover 8711.60 as far as we could see.
how_small_importers_are_coping: CSC Motorcycles (Zongshen OEM, Azusa) closed July 2026 explicitly citing tariffs + EPA (RevZilla).
Ryvid (US-assembled, imported components) raised Outset $5,995 -> $7,495 and Anthem $6,495 -> $7,995 for 2025 (cause not stated).
Kollter USA (Costa Mesa) is clearing ES1 stock at 50% off MSRP while listing a 2027 RS1 at $9,995.
Kawasaki raised Ninja e-1 from $7,599 (2026) to $7,899 (2027).
REV Rides published guidance to customers on the 20% tariff wave (Mar 2025) and warned of price hikes on Surron/Talaria/Segway/etc.
HMP's own launch-sale vs regular pricing ($5,999 vs $6,999) may reflect tariff headroom (JUDGMENT).
tariffs_and_supply.uncertainty_statement: Tariff rules changed at least five times between Mar 2025 and Jul 2026 (IEEPA fentanyl, reciprocal, Nov 2025 deal, SCOTUS Feb 2026, Section 122, forced-labor 301) and USTR/Commerce retain rolling authority to add products with 90-day reviews. Any LA-store pro forma should model landed cost at 25%, 37.5% and 60% tariff scenarios and confirm HTS treatment in writing with a broker.

implications.text: As of Sep 2026 the FLASH dual is the cheapest street-legal, shipping 70+ mph electric two-wheeler in the US at its $5,999 sale price; the only other one under $6,500 is Kollter's clearance stock in Costa Mesa. At the $6,999 regular price the claim weakens to 'cheapest among Ryvid/LAND/Kollter-MSRP'.

The addressable pool is tiny and shrinking: ~930 units nationally in the 50+hp on-road EV segment in 2025; LA County motorcycle registrations fell from 150k (2022) to 139k (2024); CA registrations fell ~3% in 2025; new-unit motorcycle sales -7.6% in 2025. 'Should sell better in SoCal' is plausible on climate, lane-splitting and delivery density, but not on market growth.

The nearest SoCal-based rivals have exited or retreated (CSC closed Jul 2026; Kollter on clearance; Ryvid +$1,500; Zero HQ to Netherlands; LiveWire cutting prices 25%). A vacuum exists, but it was created by economics (tariffs, EPA, weak demand) that apply to HMP too.

New entrants are aiming at the same slot: LiveWire S4 Honcho ($4,999-5,499, 59 mph) is arriving at H-D dealers this summer, Kawasaki e-1 sits at $7,599-7,899 with a dense dealer network, and Evoke Nrgy 6 ($4,995 target, 75 mph, 6.4 kWh) is announced for 2027. The window of 'no real rival' is likely 12-18 months (ESTIMATE).

Every press piece benchmarks FLASH against the BMW CE 04 ($12,199) and Honda PCX160 ($4,349, ~$6,500 out the door). In LA the PCX/ADV160/XMAX are the real cross-shop and are available at dozens of dealers with financing and service; the store's sales pitch must be TCO and legality (no smog, no gas, lane splitting, removable batteries for apartments), not just '75 mph for $6k'.

Trust, not price, is the identified objection: reviewers flag Luyuan OEM origin, a one-person LinkedIn footprint, AI marketing images and drop-ship fears; the only owner thread lists seven defects on a Lightning. A physical LA store with test rides, on-site service and visible parts stock directly answers the objection and is the strongest argument FOR a sales-led store.

California SB 586 (effective 2026-01-01) makes Sur-Ron/Talaria-class e-motos off-highway only; LA has one of the largest such rider populations. A DOT/CARB-certified 75 mph bike is the legal upgrade path - a marketing segment none of the established brands is chasing at this price.

Landed-cost exposure: a China-built e-moto currently faces ~37.5% stacked duties (25% 301 + 12.5% forced-labor), down from ~55%+ in mid-2025 but subject to rolling changes; spare packs face ~40%. Model the LA store at 25/37.5/60% tariff scenarios; a swing of 20 points on a ~$3k FOB bike is ~$600/unit, roughly the whole launch discount.

Realistic LA volume: if HMP captured 10-15% of a SoCal share of the ~930-unit national premium segment plus a larger slice of the sub-$7k commuter/delivery segment, first-year LA sales of 150-400 units is a defensible planning range; 1,000+ would require the delivery-fleet channel to work. (Derived from LiveWire's 653 national units with ~70% share and CSC's ~550 units/yr average across all models.)

Precedents for a D2C brand opening an LA showroom exist (Maeving Culver City, NIU Melrose, Aventura-X Carson, Kollter Costa Mesa) - all are low-volume. The store should be sized as a service-and-test-ride hub with fleet/delivery sales, not a high-traffic retail showroom; rent and staffing should assume <2 units/day.

Prioritize what FLASH loses on: publish highway-speed range, curb weight (site says 335 lb, marketing says 299), OEM/QC story, parts availability, a 3.3 kW charging default, and a resale/buy-back program. Otherwise the 75 mph headline invites the exact 'Chinese rebrand' skepticism already in comments.

Secure the 'only 75 mph under $6k' position while it lasts: lock the $5,999 dual price through 2027 if margin allows, get one mainstream test (RideApart/Cycle World/Motorcycle.com currently silent), and seed Reddit/owner content - organic discussion is absent two months after launch.
